advice.text: With 18 residuals a normality test has little power: a non-significant result does not show that the data are Gaussian, and a significant one may come from a single unusual value. Look at the QQ plot and think about the measurement itself (are values bounded, skewed, ratios or concentrations that belong on a log scale?). Do not switch test because of the normality P value alone.
advice.source: GraphPad statistics guide, 'Interpreting results: Normality tests'; Motulsky H, Intuitive Biostatistics, ch. 24 'Normality tests'; Gierlinski M, University of Dundee Data Analysis Group statistics lecture 9 'ANOVA' (dag.compbio.dundee.ac.uk). Thresholds (20 and 100 residuals) are OpenDose's choice.

result.log_note: The aligned rank transform tests ranks, so it gives no estimate in the data's units. For positive data whose SD grows with the mean (concentrations, titres, expression levels), a two-way ANOVA on the logarithms is often the better route: it keeps the interaction on a ratio scale and reports geometric means and ratios with CIs (Bland & Altman 1996, BMJ 312:770). Keep the aligned rank transform for scores and outcomes no transform makes Gaussian.

interaction_contrasts.source: Maxwell & Delaney 2004, Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data, 2nd ed., ch. 12-14 (contrasts in within-subject and split-plot designs, each with its own error term); Gelman & Stern 2006, Am Stat 60:328
interaction_contrasts.explainer: To ask whether the effect of one factor differs between the levels of the other, look at the interaction: the difference of the two effects with its CI. One effect being 'significant' and the other 'not significant' does not show that they differ (Gelman & Stern 2006).

contrast_notes: The contrasts and simple effects of a repeated-measures design are tested on the subjects' contrast scores, variance pooled across the 2 groups (df = 6 subjects - 2 groups), not on the pooled ANOVA residual, so they need no sphericity.

result.design: both factors repeated (every subject in every cell)

row_factor.hf_formula: Huynh-Feldt epsilon with Lecoutre's (1991) correction, ((N - g + 1) d GG - 2) / (d (N - g - d GG)), capped at 1 (as R car and afex)
row_factor.note: Mauchly's test is reported, not used to choose the correction: P is Geisser-Greenhouse corrected either way.

column_factor.hf_formula: Huynh-Feldt epsilon with Lecoutre's (1991) correction, ((N - g + 1) d GG - 2) / (d (N - g - d GG)), capped at 1 (as R car and afex)
column_factor.note: Mauchly's test is reported, not used to choose the correction: P is Geisser-Greenhouse corrected either way.
column_factor.mauchly_note: With 2 levels there is one contrast, so sphericity always holds (epsilon = 1).

interaction.hf_formula: Huynh-Feldt epsilon with Lecoutre's (1991) correction, ((N - g + 1) d GG - 2) / (d (N - g - d GG)), capped at 1 (as R car and afex)
interaction.note: Mauchly's test is reported, not used to choose the correction: P is Geisser-Greenhouse corrected either way.

interaction.partial_omega_squared_method: Olejnik & Algina (2003), as R effectsize::omega_squared(partial = TRUE) for designs with subjects
interaction.ci_method: noncentral F, eta_p^2 = lambda / (lambda + df1 + df2 + 1) (Steiger 2004); covers the population value that eta^2, omega^2 and epsilon^2 estimate; uncorrected df (assumes sphericity)

interaction_contrasts.p_adjustment: none (each contrast is its own question)
interaction_contrasts.error_term: the subjects' contrast scores (one-sample t, df = 3 subjects - 1)
interaction_contrasts.source: Maxwell & Delaney 2004, Designing Experiments and Analyzing Data, 2nd ed., ch. 12-14 (contrasts in within-subject and split-plot designs, each with its own error term); Gelman & Stern 2006, Am Stat 60:328
interaction_contrasts.explainer: To ask whether the effect of one factor differs between the levels of the other, look at the interaction: the difference of the two effects with its CI. One effect being 'significant' and the other 'not significant' does not show that they differ (Gelman & Stern 2006).

contrast_notes: The contrasts and simple effects of a repeated-measures design are tested on the subjects' contrast scores (one-sample t, df = 3 subjects - 1), not on the pooled ANOVA residual, so they need no sphericity.

result.sphericity_note: The mixed model assumes compound symmetry. Geisser-Greenhouse epsilon (pairwise-complete covariance of the repeated measures) multiplies both df of each repeated-measures term; the fit is unchanged. A factor with 2 levels always has epsilon = 1.

interpretation.label: medium
interpretation.source: Cohen (1988) sec. 7.2.3: w = 0.1 small, 0.3 medium, 0.5 large (Cramer's V compared as w = V sqrt(min(r, c) - 1))

result.source: exact conditional (binomial) test of the rate ratio, Przyborowski & Wilenski (1940) Biometrika 31:313; exact Poisson CI of each rate, Garwood (1936) Biometrika 28:437; as R poisson.test
